RC modeling is very underrated. Were it not for the RC industry the advance of robotics would have been at a near standstill for the past 30 years. Most robotics research relies on parts from the RC industry. And, thanks to RC, robotics has recently achieved something that only the PC industry has ever achieved before; creating a global industrial ecology. The most remarkable thing about the PC--the most sophisticated artifact ever produced by civilization--is that it's something a child can be taught to assemble in an hour from parts each made by a completely different company in a completely different country and, nine times out of ten, it will boot-up and run the first time you turn it on. Think about that. How is that even possible? It's because the computer industry evolved into a kind of ecology of developers and manufacturers simultaneously competing within the sphere of subcomponents yet following common interface standards built on an open system architecture. This was necessary because of how complex computers are. There's just too much for any one company to completely command the R&D for. And so they had spread that development across an ecology that could both stimulate competition but preclude monopoly. There is no other product or industry in the world like that, except one new one; multirotor drones. And those only exist because, some years back, a bunch of robotics students took some RC model plane parts, a new tiny microcontroller, and combined them with some motion sensors pulled out of a Wii controller. And a few years later you got thousands of companies around the world making an endless array of competing components based on a common set of multirotor designs and controller architectures--just like the PC. That's the first time that has ever happened in robotics and it could be the breakthrough that really sets robots on the course to being mainstream. This is overlooked history in the making.
